why.correct: ρ = m/V = 89.6 g / 10.0 cm³ = 8.96 g/cm³. Since 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³), ρ = 8.96 × 10³ kg/m³.
Density is a property of the material, not of the sample's size. A: 27.0/10.0 = 2.70 g/cm³; C: 54.0/20.0 = 2.70 g/cm³. Same density, likely the same metal (aluminum has 2.70 g/cm³).
options: Right: C has twice the mass and twice the volume of A, so the same density.
A has 2.70 g/cm³ and B has 8.96 g/cm³: same volume, very different masses.
B has 8.96 g/cm³ and D has 19.3 g/cm³.
C has 2.70 g/cm³ and D has 19.3 g/cm³; D's small volume makes its mass misleading.

why.correct: Cutting reduces mass and volume in the same ratio, so m/V does not change. Density belongs to the material.
options: Right: density does not depend on how much of the material you have.
The smaller piece has one third of the mass and one third of the volume, so the ratio is unchanged.
Halving would need the mass to drop without the volume dropping.
Both mass and volume shrink by the same factor.

why.correct: Squeezing changed the air's volume noticeably but not the water's. Liquids are close to incompressible because their particles are already touching; gas particles are far apart.
options: Right: water's volume hardly changes under the push.
Not leaking does not make a fluid incompressible; the air's volume clearly shrank.
This reverses the observations: the air plunger moved in.
A fluid is defined by flowing and taking its container's shape, which both do.

why.correct: The blocked tip keeps the mass of air fixed, while the volume shrinks. ρ = m/V, so the density rises. A compressible fluid's density can change.
options: Right: same m, smaller V, larger ρ.
The mass stays the same, but density is mass per volume and the volume shrank.
Pushing the plunger in squeezes the particles closer together, not farther apart.
For an incompressible fluid density is fixed, but air is compressible.

why.correct: An ideal fluid is incompressible (constant density) and nonviscous (no internal friction), and its flow is smooth and steady.
options: Right: incompressible means constant density.
Sticking to walls is a sign of viscosity, which an ideal fluid lacks.
An ideal fluid has mass and weight; only its friction is ignored.
No fluid keeps its shape; that is the difference between a fluid and a solid.

why.correct: In a liquid the particles touch and slide past each other; there is little empty space to squeeze out. In a gas most of the volume is empty space between particles.
options: Right: the spacing of the particles decides how compressible the fluid is.
Water particles can slide past each other; that is why water flows.
The two syringes hold the same volume; the difference is in particle spacing, not mass.
In a gas the attractions between particles are weak, which is why they spread out.

why.correct: A fluid is a substance that flows and takes the shape of its container: a liquid or a gas. Honey flows, slowly.
options: Right: honey is a liquid, so it is a fluid (a viscous one).
Steel keeps its own shape: a solid.
Ice is solid water; it keeps its shape until it melts.
A rubber band can stretch but keeps a shape of its own; it does not flow.

why.correct: V = 10.0 m × 5.0 m × 2.0 m = 100 m³. m = ρV = (1000 kg/m³)(100 m³) = 1.0 × 10⁵ kg, about 100 metric tons.
Same material, same density. Volume = side³, so doubling the side gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and m = ρV gives 8 times the mass.
options: Right: volume, and so mass, goes as the cube of the side.
This treats the volume as proportional to the side length.
This uses the area of one face (side²) instead of the volume.
Density is the same, but a bigger cube contains more material.

why.correct: ρ = m/V. The bottle is sealed (same mass) and rigid (same volume), so the density is unchanged even though the particles move faster.
options: Right: density depends only on mass and volume.
Faster particles raise the pressure, not the mass or volume.
Warm air is less dense only when it is free to expand; this bottle is sealed and rigid.
The pressure does rise, but density is mass per volume, which has not changed.

why.correct: V = 250 cm³ = 250 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³. ρ = m/V = 0.229 kg / 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 916 kg/m³, a little less than water.
Density is a property of the material; mass and volume depend on how much material there is.

variables.name: Mass
variables.why: Half the material, so half the mass.

variables.name: Volume
variables.why: Half the material takes up half the space.

variables.name: Density
variables.why: Mass and volume both halve, so their ratio ρ = m/V does not change.

why.correct: In both solids and liquids the particles are close together, but in a liquid they are not locked in place, so the liquid flows.
options: Right: particles that slide past each other make a fluid.
Particles far apart describe a gas; liquids are nearly incompressible.
Liquid particles attract each other; that is what holds a drop together.
The particles keep moving even when the liquid as a whole is still.

why.correct: In a fluid at rest, pressure depends only on depth: P = P₀ + ρgh. J and K are both 1.5 m down, so their pressures are equal, whatever the tank's shape.
options: Right: equal depth, equal pressure.
Distance from a wall does not appear in P = P₀ + ρgh.
The same depth of water lies above both points.
At a point, a fluid pushes equally in every direction; that does not change the pressure from J to K.

why.correct: P_gauge = ρgh = (1000 kg/m³)(9.8 m/s²)(4.5 m) = 4.4 × 10⁴ Pa. This is what a pressure gauge, which reads zero in open air, would show.

The gauge pressure ρgh triples (1.47 × 10⁴ Pa to 4.41 × 10⁴ Pa), but the absolute pressure also includes P₀ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, which is the same at both. So P goes from 1.15 × 10⁵ Pa to 1.44 × 10⁵ Pa, a factor of about 1.3.
options: Right: only the ρgh part triples; P₀ does not.
This would be true of the gauge pressure, not the absolute pressure.
Pressure grows linearly with depth, not with depth squared.
Constant density is what makes P grow steadily with depth; it does not make P constant.

why.correct: At the surface the absolute pressure equals atmospheric pressure, about 101 kPa. Gauge pressure would read zero there.
options: Right: the intercept is P₀.
The reading at the surface is real: the atmosphere presses on the water.
The graph rises with depth; pressure increases as you go down.
A gauge reading would start at zero; the diver's weight does not enter.

why.correct: P = P₀ + ρgh, so the slope of P against h is ρg. Slope = (199 kPa − 101 kPa)/(10 m) = 9.8 kPa/m = 9800 Pa/m. ρ = 9800 Pa/m ÷ 9.8 m/s² = 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³.
The intercept is the atmospheric pressure, which does not depend on the water. The slope is ρg, which is larger for denser water.
options: Right: P₀ is unchanged; ρg is larger.
The surface reading is the air's pressure, not the water's.
Denser water adds more pressure per meter of depth.
The intercept is set by the atmosphere, not by the water.

why.correct: Consider a column of water: each layer must hold up the weight of the water above it (plus the air). The deeper the layer, the more weight above, so the larger the pressure. ρgh is that extra weight per unit area.
options: Right: pressure at depth holds up the column above.
Water is nearly incompressible; its density barely changes with depth.
Pressure is a scalar; a fluid at a point pushes equally in all directions.
Colder particles move more slowly; temperature is not the cause here.

why.correct: P = F⊥/A = 600 N / 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 4.0 × 10⁶ Pa, about 40 times atmospheric pressure. The same weight on a flat shoe of 150 cm² gives only 4.0 × 10⁴ Pa.

P = F⊥/A is a scalar measured in pascals (N/m²). Pressure has no direction of its own; the force it exerts on any surface is perpendicular to that surface, which is why water pushes sideways on a dam.
options: Right: scalar pressure, perpendicular force.
Water pushes sideways on walls and up on the bottom of a submerged object, so the force is not always down.
At a point in a fluid, the push is the same in every direction.
Pressure is force per area (Pa), not force (N), and not weight.

why.correct: Pressure in a fluid at rest depends only on depth: P = P₀ + ρgh. Same depth of the same liquid, same pressure, whatever the amount or shape.
options: Right: only depth (and ρ and g) set the pressure.
More water means more total weight, but it is spread over a larger bottom area; the pressure is the same.
Narrowness does not concentrate pressure; depth decides.
The walls do push on the water, but the result is still P = P₀ + ρgh.

why.correct: P = P₀ + P_gauge = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa + 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa = 3.2 × 10⁵ Pa. A flat tire reads 0 on the gauge but still holds air at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
P = P₀ + ρgh, so ρgh = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa − 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa = 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa and h = 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa / (1000 kg/m³ × 9.8 m/s²) = 5.1 m. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere.
Gauge pressure in a fluid at rest is ρgh: it depends on the fluid's density, g and the depth.

variables.name: The submarine dives to 40 m
variables.why: P_gauge = ρgh: twice the depth gives twice the gauge pressure.

variables.name: The window is made twice as large, at 20 m
variables.why: Pressure depends on depth, not on the area; a larger window feels a larger force, F = PA, at the same pressure.

variables.name: The submarine moves to fresh water, at 20 m
variables.why: Fresh water is less dense than seawater, so ρgh is smaller.

why.correct: The pressure at a tap below the tower is larger by ρgh, where h is the height of the water surface above the tap. A taller tower means larger h and more pressure.
options: Right: pressure grows with the depth below the water surface.
The amount of water is not what sets the pressure; height is.
Water is pushed, not pulled: the higher pressure is at the bottom.
The tower is open to the air; the height of water is what matters.

why.correct: In air the scale holds the whole weight, 2.65 N. Fully under water it reads 1.67 N, because the water pushes up with the rest: F_b = 2.65 N − 1.67 N = 0.98 N. Check: ρVg = (1000)(1.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³)(9.8) = 0.98 N.

F_b = ρ_fluid V_displaced g. Once the cylinder is all under water, V_displaced equals its full volume and cannot grow. The pressures on the top and bottom both rise with depth, but their difference stays the same.
options: Right: the buoyant force follows the displaced volume.
Pressure keeps rising with depth; it is the difference between the bottom and top pressures that stays fixed.
The weight mg does not change in water; the scale reading changes because the buoyant force supports part of it.
A bigger object would displace more water and feel a larger buoyant force.

why.correct: Fully submerged, F_b = ρ_w V g and the weight is ρ_cyl V g. Dividing, ρ_cyl/ρ_w = W/F_b = 2.65 N / 0.98 N = 2.70, so ρ_cyl = 2.7 × 10³ kg/m³ (aluminum).
F_b = ρ_fluid V g: the same displaced volume of a denser fluid weighs more, so the buoyant force is larger and the scale has less weight left to support.
options: Right: denser fluid, larger buoyant force, smaller reading.
Salt water pushes harder on both the top and the bottom; the upward push on the bottom grows more.
Same volume, but the buoyant force depends on the fluid's density too.
The gravitational force on the cylinder, mg, does not depend on the fluid around it.

why.correct: Two forces act up on the cylinder (the scale's tension and the water's buoyant force) and one down (Earth's gravitational force). At rest the net force is zero: F_T + F_b = F_g.
options: Right: up forces balance the down force.
This puts the buoyant force downward; it acts upward, opposite to gravity.
This leaves out the scale's pull; the cylinder would sink without it.
This leaves out the buoyant force, so the reading would equal the weight.

why.correct: F_b = ρ_water V_displaced g. Z displaces its whole volume, Y three quarters, X one half. The blocks have equal volumes, so Z > Y > X.
options: Right: more displaced water, larger buoyant force.
This reverses the ranking; floating higher means less water displaced.
Equal volumes are not equal displaced volumes: X and Y are only partly under water.
Z, fully under water, displaces the most.

why.correct: Floating at rest, F_b = F_g: ρ_w V_sub g = ρ_X V g, so ρ_X = ρ_w (V_sub/V) = 1000 kg/m³ × ½ = 500 kg/m³.
Y is at rest with only two forces on it, so they balance: F_b = F_g. Floating means the buoyant force equals the weight, not that it exceeds it.
options: Right: equilibrium of a floating object.
If F_b were larger, Y would accelerate upward until it displaced less water.
Being partly out of the water lowers F_b only until it matches the weight.
Y is denser than X, which is why it sits lower; it still floats with F_b = F_g.

why.correct: Z displaces its full volume, so it does feel a buoyant force, but Z is denser than water, so F_b < F_g. At rest, F_b + F_N = F_g.
options: Right: three forces balance on the sunk block.
The model treats the water as pushing up on Z, giving a buoyant force ρVg; the floor adds a normal force.
At rest the net force is zero, but the normal force is part of the balance.
The buoyant force depends on the displaced volume, not the block's density: Z displaces the most.

why.correct: Floating, X displaced half its volume; fully under, it displaces all of it. F_b ∝ V_displaced, so it doubles. The extra push comes from the hand.
options: Right: twice the displaced volume, twice the buoyant force.
The buoyant force depends on how much water is displaced, which doubled.
Pushing it deeper displaces more water, not less.
The displaced volume doubled, so the force doubles, not quadruples.

why.correct: F_b = ρ_water V_displaced g = (1000 kg/m³)(3.0 × 10⁻³ m³)(9.8 m/s²) = 29 N. The rock's own density does not enter.
F_b = ρ_fluid V_displaced g depends on the fluid and the displaced volume, not on the object. The lead sinks because its weight is larger, not because its buoyant force is different.
options: Right: same displaced volume, same buoyant force.
Both displace exactly their own volume when fully submerged; weight does not change that.
Density decides whether an object floats, not the size of the buoyant force when submerged.
Both are held at the same depth here; and once submerged, depth does not change F_b.

why.correct: Floating: F_b = F_g, so ρ_w V_sub g = ρ_ice V g and V_sub/V = 917/1000 = 0.917. About 92% of the ice is under water.
Floating, F_b = mg: ρ_w V g = mg, so V = m/ρ_w = 0.60 kg / 1000 kg/m³ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. A floating object displaces its own mass of fluid.
Newton's second law, down positive: ma = mg − ρ_w V g. With m = ρ_s V, a = g(1 − ρ_w/ρ_s) = 9.8 m/s² × (1 − 1000/7800) = 8.5 m/s².
A floating object displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.

variables.name: Buoyant force on the barge
variables.why: Floating means F_b equals the total weight, which increased.

variables.name: Volume of water the barge displaces
variables.why: A larger buoyant force needs more displaced water: the barge sits lower.

variables.name: Density of the river water
variables.why: The water is incompressible; loading the barge does not change it.

why.correct: The surrounding water does not know what is inside the boundary. It pushes on the parcel exactly as it would push on the stone. The parcel is at rest (Newton's first law), so that push equals the parcel's weight, ρ_w V g.
options: Right: same boundary, same push, and for the parcel that push balances its weight.
The parcel has weight; it is held up by the buoyant force.
Pressure grows with depth; that difference is what makes the buoyant force.
The water parcel does not sink; it is at rest.

why.correct: Volume flow rate = A₁v₁ = (4.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(1.5 m/s) = 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³/s, six liters each second. It is the same at every section of the pipe.
Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = (4.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(1.5 m/s)/(1.0 × 10⁻³ m²) = 6.0 m/s. A quarter of the area, four times the speed.
Bernoulli with y₁ = y₂ (horizontal pipe): P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂². P₂ = 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa + ½(1000 kg/m³)[(1.5 m/s)² − (6.0 m/s)²] = 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa − 1.69 × 10⁴ Pa = 1.83 × 10⁵ Pa.

Water speeds up from section 1 to section 2, so it gains kinetic energy. A net force must act on it in the direction of flow, which means the pressure behind it (section 1) is larger than the pressure ahead (section 2).
options: Right: faster flow, lower pressure in a horizontal pipe.
This "squeezing" picture is the classic error; the water accelerates into the narrow part, so the pressure there is lower.
Incompressible means constant density, not constant pressure.
The same flow rate through less area means higher speed, which goes with lower pressure.

why.correct: The volume flowing in each second must flow out (an incompressible fluid cannot pile up), so A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ gives v₂ from the areas alone. Bernoulli, an energy statement, then turns the speed change into a pressure change.
options: Right: geometry and continuity first, then energy.
Bernoulli has two unknowns here (P₂ and v₂); continuity has to supply the speed.
One equation cannot give two unknowns.
Continuity says nothing about pressure.

why.correct: Bernoulli from the surface (point 1) to the hole (point 2): both are open to the air, so P₁ = P₂ = P₀; the surface barely moves, so v₁ ≈ 0. Then ρgy₁ = ρgy₂ + ½ρv², and v = √(2g × 1.8 m) = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.8) m/s = 5.9 m/s (Torricelli's result).
A_surface v_surface = A_hole v_hole. With A_surface much larger than A_hole, v_surface is tiny, and ½ρv² there is negligible.
options: Right: continuity makes the surface speed negligible.
Pressure does not stop motion; the surface is falling, just slowly.
The surface does not gain or lose height quickly; this is not why its speed is small.
The water level is dropping, so the water in the tank moves; just slowly.

why.correct: v = √(2gh), so v ∝ √h. Four times the depth (7.2/1.8 = 4) gives √4 = 2 times the speed.
options: Right: speed grows as the square root of depth.
This treats v as proportional to h; it is proportional to √h.
The depth is 4 times as large, not 2 times.
Deeper water is at higher pressure and pushes the jet out faster.

why.correct: The exit speed √(2gh) depends only on the depth, not on the hole's size. The flow rate Av then halves with A.
options: Right: v from depth, then flow rate = Av.
A garden-hose nozzle speeds water up because a pump keeps the flow rate fixed; here the depth fixes the speed instead.
Nothing about the speed formula involves the hole's area.
The speed is set by the depth; with less area the flow rate cannot grow.

why.correct: Flow rate = Av = (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²)(5.94 m/s) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³/s, about 1.2 liters per second.
The supply pushes water through at about the same volume flow rate. Continuity, Av = constant, means a smaller opening needs a larger speed.
options: Right: continuity.
Your thumb is at rest, so it does no work on the water.
This is the "squeezed water has higher pressure" error. Once it leaves, the jet is at atmospheric pressure; it is faster because the same flow passes a smaller opening.
Water is nearly incompressible; continuity, not compression, explains the jet.

why.correct: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ with A₂ = A₁/3, so v₂ = 3v₁ = 0.90 m/s.

Continuity: constant area means equal speeds, so the ½ρv² terms cancel in Bernoulli's equation. P_low − P_high = ρgΔy = (1000 kg/m³)(9.8 m/s²)(5.0 m) = 4.9 × 10⁴ Pa; the lower point has the higher pressure.

Each term is an energy per unit volume: ½ρv² (kinetic), ρgy (gravitational potential), and P (the work done per unit volume by the pressure pushing the fluid along). With no friction (an ideal fluid), their sum stays constant along the flow.
options: Right: energy per unit volume.
Mass conservation is the continuity equation, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Momentum conservation is not what Bernoulli expresses.
Bernoulli involves no rotation.

why.correct: Continuity sets the speeds from the areas; Bernoulli then gives the pressure change.

variables.name: Volume flow rate
variables.why: Continuity: what flows in each second flows out; the fluid is incompressible.

variables.name: Speed of the water
variables.why: Twice the diameter is four times the area, so the speed is a quarter as large.

variables.name: Pressure in the water
variables.why: Bernoulli, same height: the water slows down, so its pressure rises.

why.correct: Gravity speeds the water up. The volume flow rate Av is the same at every height, so where v is larger, A must be smaller.
options: Right: faster flow, smaller area.
Air pressure is about the same all along the short stream.
Water is nearly incompressible.
Evaporation over a fraction of a second is negligible.
